tier_reason: doc/Benchmarks.md (Win32.VC71.MS.Release table, EASTL 0.96.00) is a first-party EA table against the VC++ 7.1 Dinkumware std::basic_string, and every claimed ratio appears in it; no CPU model, exact flags or variance are given. N2271 (also first-party, by EASTL's author) names flags but only the CPU family (Pentium 4), and the 0.96-era harness is not the code in today's repo, so it falls short of A.

(exact flags not given), PPMalloc::GeneralAllocator, thread safety enabled; also a VC++ 7.1 + STLport column. N2271 appendix 20: Windows column VC8 -Og -Oi -Ot -Oy -Ob2 -GF -Gy with the compiler-supplied STL; console column VC7 -Ox -Ob2 -Oi -Os on 64-bit PowerPC; Linux column GCC 4.1 -O3 with libstdc++; Mac column GCC 4.0 -Os with libstdc++ on a G5.
corrections.caveats: The only published tables are doc/Benchmarks.md (EASTL version 0.96.00, Windows x86, Microsoft Visual C++ 7.1 with the Dinkumware STL or STLport, custom PPMalloc allocator, no CPU model stated) and the 2007 WG21 paper N2271 (doc/EASTL-n2271.pdf, written by EASTL's author), so all numbers are first-party and roughly 20 years old. Ratios are other-STL time divided by EASTL time from a single stopwatch run in CPU cycles, with no variance reported, and the ratio printer caps at 100.00 (the STLport and N2271 Linux/Mac reserve rows read exactly 100.00; e.g. STLport char8_t reserve is 672517501 vs 78387 cycles). The reserve rows (10.73x char8_t, 4.87x char16_t vs Dinkumware) measure a semantic difference rather than a faster reserve: benchmark/source/BenchmarkString.cpp calls reserve with capacity-2 .. capacity+1 in rotation, which the old Dinkumware, STLport and libstdc++ strings honoured as shrink or regrow requests (reallocating), while EASTL's reserve never shrinks. Against STLport in Release the string gains mostly vanish: push_back 1.33x/1.34x, find_first_not_of 2.41x/2.30x, find/find_first_of/find_last_of/operator[] about 1.00x, and char16_t compare 0.82x and swap 0.90x (EASTL slower). The harness pre-sizes every string to 16 characters, so it does not measure the small-string optimization that today's include/EASTL/string.h has (SSOLayout); the published rows describe the 0.96 implementation, not today's code. The baselines are the 2005 Dinkumware string, STLport and, in N2271's Linux column, the copy-on-write std::string of libstdc++ 4.1 (GCC 4.1 -O3), none of which is a modern libstdc++ new-ABI, libc++ or current MSVC string, so the speedups are probably much smaller today. N2271 Linux column (Pentium 4, GCC 4.1 -O3): char8_t push_back 2.28x, find 5.06x, find_first_of 10.11x, find_last_of 8.27x, rfind 8.70x, insert 0.77x. N2271 Windows column (VC8): char8_t push_back 2.28x but find 0.58x. char8_t in the benchmark source is EABase's 8-bit char typedef (the suite does not compile with C++20 char8_t, see benchmark/CMakeLists.txt). eastl::fixed_string has no published numbers. No comparison against folly fbstring exists in the repo, and no independent eastl::string vs std::string measurement was found (one WebSearch; a Stack Overflow anecdote reports EASTL slower for push_back of short strings into a vector, without methodology).

notes: All claimed ratios match the Win32.VC71.MS.Release table and the N2271 Linux column exactly. Shortcomings to record: first-party 2005-2007 numbers against Dinkumware/STLport/libstdc++ 4.1 COW strings; the biggest reserve wins come from a harness that issues shrink requests EASTL ignores; gains vs STLport Release are about 1.0x except push_back (1.33x) and find_first_not_of (2.4x); harness pre-sizes to 16 chars so SSO is not measured. Metadata checked: BSD-3-Clause, 9.4k stars, 1.0k forks, last commit 2025-10-29 (active).

corrections.caveats: Tier D: no numbers anywhere, and no sign that the author claims a speed win over std::string or std::sort; the value is heap-free, fixed-capacity strings with predictable latency. The README's only performance-related line is a design statement ('Cache Efficiency: Containers use contiguous memory layouts for optimal cache performance'), not a comparison. docs/utilities/algorithms.md lists the functions and says nothing about speed, and docs/blog has no performance post. Kept as a placeholder record in case a user benchmark appears; the container record for the same repo has the only existing timing harness (test/Performance/unordered_map, no results). Three WebSearch queries for independent etl::string or ETL timings found nothing.

N2271 appendix 20: Windows column VC8 -Og -Oi -Ot -Oy -Ob2 -GF -Gy with the compiler-supplied STL; console column VC7 -Ox -Ob2 -Oi -Os on 64-bit PowerPC; Linux column GCC 4.1 -O3 with libstdc++; Mac column GCC 4.0 -Os with libstdc++ on a G5.
corrections.caveats: The only published tables are doc/Benchmarks.md (EASTL version 0.96.00, Windows x86, Microsoft Visual C++ 7.1 with the Dinkumware STL or STLport, custom PPMalloc allocator, no CPU model stated) and the 2007 WG21 paper N2271 (doc/EASTL-n2271.pdf, written by EASTL's author), so all numbers are first-party and roughly 20 years old. Ratios are other-STL time divided by EASTL time from a single stopwatch run in CPU cycles, with no variance reported. Against STLport's std::sort in Release the gain is small: random input 1.00x-1.12x, already-sorted 1.25x-1.38x. N2271 columns: Linux (Pentium 4, GCC 4.1 -O3, libstdc++) 0.96x (vector<uint32> random) to 1.34x (vector<TestObject> sorted); Windows VC8 1.25x-1.50x; Mac G5 GCC 4.0 -Os 1.14x-1.75x; console PowerPC VC7 1.49x-3.53x. Against libstdc++'s sort the gain was small. The std::sort implementations of 2005-2007 are far behind current libstdc++, libc++ and MSVC introsorts, so the 1.7-1.9x vs Dinkumware does not transfer. radix_sort: include/EASTL/sort.h only says it is 'typically faster than any other sort' and 'faster than all others' for integral data (qualitative). The current benchmark/source/BenchmarkSort.cpp compares eastl::sort (quick_sort), radix_sort, tim_sort, merge_sort, heap_sort and others against std::sort and std::stable_sort at sizes 10, 100, 1000 and 10000 over random, random-sorted, ordered and mostly-ordered input, but only at verbosity 3, it prints its tables at run time and no results are checked in; no independent radix_sort measurement was found. eastl::copy is in the same family: Benchmarks.md release rows give algorithm/copy/vector<LargePOD> 1.30x and copy/vector<uint32_t> 0.91x (EASTL slower), so no copy win is claimed.

notes: All claimed ratios match the Win32.VC71.MS.Release sort/q_sort rows; the harness calls std::sort vs eastl::quick_sort on 10000-element inputs (BenchmarkSort.cpp), and eastl::sort maps to quick_sort unless EASTL_DEFAULT_SORT_FUNCTION is set. Shortcomings to record: first-party 2005-2007 numbers vs Dinkumware std::sort; EASTL slower on already-sorted TestObject (0.55x/0.59x); vs STLport and libstdc++ 4.1 roughly 1.0x-1.3x; no radix_sort numbers.
